title: Two Sum

solutions.explanation: The brute force approach checks every possible pair of numbers in the array. For each number at index i, we check all numbers that come after it (index j where j > i) to see if they sum to the target. This guarantees we find the solution if it exists, but is inefficient for large arrays.

solutions.code:
def twoSum(nums: list[int], target: int) -> list[int]:
    """
    Optimal approach using hash map for O(n) time complexity.
    """
    seen = {}  # Map: number -> index
    
    for i, num in enumerate(nums):
        complement = target - num
        if complement in seen:
            return [seen[complement], i]
        seen[num] = i
    
    return []
solutions.explanation: The hash map approach makes a single pass through the array. For each number, we calculate its complement (target - num) and check if we've seen it before. If we have, we've found our pair! If not, we store the current number and its index in the hash map for future lookups. This trades space for time - we use O(n) extra space but achieve O(n) time complexity.

key_insights: Hash maps can trade space for time complexity - a common optimization pattern
The 'complement' pattern: for pair problems, store what you've seen and check for target - current
One-pass solutions are often possible when you track information as you go
Consider whether you need the values or the indices - this problem asks for indices
edge_cases: Empty array - problem guarantees at least 2 elements, but good to consider
Array with exactly 2 elements - simplest valid case
Negative numbers - solution works for any integers
Duplicate numbers - hash map handles this correctly
No solution exists - problem guarantees exactly one solution

title: Valid Parentheses

solutions.code:
def isValid(s: str) -> bool:
    """
    Use a stack to match opening and closing brackets.
    """
    stack = []
    mapping = {')': '(', '}': '{', ']': '['}
    
    for char in s:
        if char in mapping:  # Closing bracket
            if not stack or stack[-1] != mapping[char]:
                return False
            stack.pop()
        else:  # Opening bracket
            stack.append(char)
    
    return len(stack) == 0
solutions.explanation: The stack approach uses a last-in-first-out (LIFO) data structure to match brackets. When we encounter an opening bracket, we push it onto the stack. When we encounter a closing bracket, we check if the top of the stack contains the matching opening bracket. If it does, we pop the stack. If it doesn't (or the stack is empty), the string is invalid. After processing all characters, a valid string will have an empty stack.

key_insights: Stacks are perfect for problems involving matching pairs or nested structures
LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) property naturally matches the nesting behavior of parentheses
Use a hash map to quickly look up matching bracket pairs
An empty stack at the end confirms all brackets were properly matched
Early termination: return false immediately when a mismatch is found
edge_cases: Single character - must return false (unpaired bracket)
Only opening brackets - stack won't be empty at end
Only closing brackets - stack will be empty when trying to match
Mismatched pairs like '([)]' - correct bracket types but wrong nesting order
Odd length strings - cannot be valid (impossible to pair all brackets)
